title: What changed across five public administration journals?
dek: Explore where topics gained or lost ground across {papers} papers and why some parts of the map are easier to interpret than others.

steps.text: How do the papers fit together? Every dot represents a paper. Nearby papers tend to use similar language in their titles and available abstracts. Colours mark groups fitted in the full embedding space.

The 10 broad groups cover recurring questions about governing, managing public organisations and delivering services. Read the labels as descriptions of the papers grouped together. A study can still speak to several topics.

sections.interlude: Which topics gained a larger share?

sections.vizTitle: Topic share across the five current journals

steps.text: Compare 2001–2005 with 2021–2025. The earlier cohort contains 939 papers with 93% usable abstract coverage. The later cohort contains 2,016 papers with 98% coverage. Each plotted point pools nearby years to show the longer pattern.

{theme:3} rose from 84 of 939 papers (8.9%) to 382 of 2,016 (18.9%). Its share increased in every journal. The pooled rise also appears using title-only assignments (+8.0 percentage points) and among papers with usable abstracts (+9.7).
{theme:1} rose from 78 papers (8.3%) to 322 (16.0%). The pooled rise persists with title-only assignments (+6.5 percentage points) and with the abstract-bearing subset (+7.6).

{theme:0} moved in the other direction, from 248 papers (26.4%) to 143 (7.1%). Its share fell in all five journals. The magnitude depends on the input, with a fall of 12.3 points using titles and 20.6 among papers with abstracts.

sections.interlude: Where does the map need closer reading?

sections.vizTitle: A mixed group with short records

steps.text: {theme:8} gathers 678 mixed records, of which 170 have a usable abstract. Some title-only papers group together because of generic wording. Follow their source links before interpreting them as a coherent research area.

Across the map, using titles alone and assigning papers to the same fitted groups reproduces 71% of broad group assignments. Among papers that originally had an abstract, agreement is 66%. The period comparisons above use patterns that retain their direction under both sensitivity checks.

end.title: Follow a topic to the papers behind it
